newsitem.title: USA: OPINION - Unacceptable answers on Cleveland deal.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Unacceptable answers on Cleveland deal.

text.p: By Joe Mysak, editor, Grant's Municipal Bond Observer

NEW YORK, Sept 9 - This is what we know: On August 22, Grigsby, Brandford & Co. priced $81.3 million in parking facilities revenue refunding bonds for the city of Cleveland. The issue was insured by MBIA, and yielded from 3.90% in 1997 out to 5.73% in a term bond maturing in 2022.

Then something happened. As the city's finance director, Kathryn Hyer, told us late last month: "We were unable to execute the bond purchase agreement. That's all I'm going to tell you about it. That's all there is to say about that." Before we could do that Bryant Gumbel thing, repeating the facts of the case and concluding on a punctuating "why?" she hung up. Hyer thereafter declined our calls altogether.

Another thing we know is that the words "we were unable to execute the bond purchase agreement" do not mean anything. They don't tell us anything, and they are unacceptable as an answer from a public servant. That is especially so in this instance because a week later, on August 28, Cleveland apparently sold the same bonds, this time using Smith Barney as its underwriter. However, because the market was not quite so robust as it had been the week before, the serial bonds were priced to yield from 4% in 1997 out to 5.70% in 2013, with two term bonds priced to yield 5.787% in 2016 and 5.838% in 2022.

What all this means is that Cleveland taxpayers have to cough up a little bit more. Finance director Hyer told Karen Pierog of Reuters that the difference was $500,000. A banker we spoke with said he thought it was more like $988,200. This is not chicken feed, and we wondered what happened.

According to several of our sources on the buy side of this deal, Grigsby priced and repriced it on August 23, and received the verbal award. Underwriters at the firm decided, however, to wait until the next day to allot the bonds to the other members of the syndicate. One source said the underwriters believed that the market would improve following the Friday release of the July durable goods report. But the report showed that orders for durable goods increased during the month by 1.6%, which caused municipal bond prices to drop more than a half-point. Grigsby was left holding the bag. At which point, the record shows, the firm bailed out. This we know.

What we do not know is why the city, when asked exactly what happened, pulled what Muhammad Ali used to call the rope-a-dope. Perhaps this is just the beginning of a trend, where all issuers defend their underwriters. Somehow, we don't think so.

Neither Calvin Grigsby nor Napoleon Brandford, the principals of the firm that bears their names, returned our telephone calls. We thought this more than a little interesting, too, especially because they have been rather vociferous about their firm in the past, not just to us, but to anyone who would listen. Grigsby Brandford, incidentally, ranked 27th in the nation for the first eight months of 1996, having underwritten 48 issues totaling $865 million.

It is hard to generate public outrage in the municipal market because it is so easy to snow all the people all the time by saying how "complex" things are. We are not talking about brain surgery here, but it is alarmingly easy to dismiss reporters with words such as "we were unable to execute the bond purchase agreement," and then leave it at that. We suppose if pressed, the Cleveland officials would have told us that we would not understand. What is easy to understand, however, especially from the public's point of view, is a half-million or a million bucks. What happened to it? We don't know, and neither do the people of Cleveland.
(Note - The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters.)
